Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). Derivatives are componentwise, with the multi-index and all-ordered-partials conventions of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The union of the two compact component supports is compact. A measurable complex $f$ is **locally integrable** for Lebesgue measure if $\int_K|f|<\infty$ on every compact $K$. The component inequalities give the equivalent componentwise condition. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], closed bounded balls are compact and each compact set is bounded. Hence compact integrability implies integrability on every bounded open ball by restriction from its closure; conversely each compact set is contained in a bounded open ball. These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

For the following illustration assume [[def-countable-choice]]. For $f=\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}$ on $\mathbb R$, [[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]] gives $f=0$ Lebesgue-a.e.; therefore $N_\infty(f)=0$ and $\operatorname{ess\,supp}f=\varnothing$, since $U=\mathbb R$ occurs in the union. But [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]] gives $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}=\mathbb R$. For the Dirac probability measure at zero ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), the bound $1$ holds everywhere and every $0\le M<1$ fails on $\{0\}$, of measure one. Thus $N_{\infty,\delta_0}(f)=1$.

The raw $L^2$ pairing convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$, linear in the first variable. Its integrability and class invariance are obligations of the later pairing items. **Bilinear tests** instead use $\int fs$, with no conjugation of $s$.

$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

$$\|f\|_\infty\le M.$$

derivations.claim: By [F11] and AC, $X=L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ is a Banach space. Normalize $D$ to the probability measure $d\nu=dx/M$. By [F2], the operator $K_k$ is unitarily equivalent to the integral operator on $L^2(D,\nu)$ with kernel $\widetilde a=M a$. Its kernel norm equals $\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D,dx\,dy)}$ by [F2]. Applying [F3] to this probability-space kernel gives compactness of the normalized operator and its norm bound; unitary equivalence transfers both to $K_k$.

We also verify the singular-truncation route. By [F12], choose a measurable representative $q_0$ and set it to zero on the measurable null set where $|q_0|>\|q\|_\infty$. This does not change the operator, since the kernel changes only on a product-null set, and now $|q_0(y)|\le\|q\|_\infty$ for every $y$. For $\varepsilon>0$, put $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=0$ for $r\le\varepsilon$, $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=(r-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon<r<2\varepsilon$, and $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=1$ for $r\ge2\varepsilon$. Let $K_\varepsilon$ have kernel $\chi_\varepsilon(|x-y|)G_k(x-y)q_0(y)$. The difference kernel is supported where $|x-y|<2\varepsilon$ and bounded in modulus by $\|q\|_\infty/(4\pi|x-y|)$. By [F9] its row and column integrals, for every fixed row and column, are at most $A=B\le(\|q\|_\infty/(4\pi))4\pi\int_0^{2\varepsilon}r\,dr=2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2$. For each $x$, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|T_hv(x)|^2\le(\int|h(x,y)|dy)(\int|h(x,y)||v(y)|^2dy)$; integrating and using Tonelli yields $\|T_hv\|_2^2\le AB\|v\|_2^2$. Hence $\|K-K_\varepsilon\|\le2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Extend the everywhere-bounded representative $q_0$ by zero to $\mathbb R^3$; it lies in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ because $q\in L^\infty(D)$ and $|D|<\infty$. By [F5], choose $q_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with $\|q_j-q_0\|_{L^2(D)}\to0$. The kernel $g_{\varepsilon,j}(x,y)=\chi_\varepsilon(|x-y|)G_k(x-y)q_j(y)$ extends continuously to the compact set $\overline D\times\overline D$ by assigning zero on $x=y$; the cutoff vanishes near the diagonal. For $\|v\|_2\le1$, the integral is independent of the representative of $v$, and by [F13] its outputs obey $|T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x)|\le\sqrt{|D|}\|g_{\varepsilon,j}\|_\infty$ and $|T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x)-T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x')|\le\sqrt{|D|}\sup_y|g_{\varepsilon,j}(x,y)-g_{\varepsilon,j}(x',y)|$. Uniform continuity of $g_{\varepsilon,j}$ makes these outputs uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Applying [F6] separately to real and imaginary parts gives compact closures $C_R,C_I$ in $C(\overline D;\mathbb R)$. The product $C_R\times C_I$ is compact by finite-product compactness. Under the homeomorphism $w\mapsto(\operatorname{Re}w,\operatorname{Im}w)$, the closure of the complex output family is a closed subset of this compact product, hence compact in $C(\overline D;\mathbb C)$. The inclusion is continuous because $\|w|_D\|_2\le\sqrt{|D|}\|w\|_{C(\overline D)}$; hence $T_{\varepsilon,j}:L^2(D)\to L^2(D)$ is compact.

Since $|\chi_\varepsilon G_k|\le(4\pi\varepsilon)^{-1}$, the square norm of the kernel difference between $K_\varepsilon$ and $T_{\varepsilon,j}$ is at most $|D|(16\pi^2\varepsilon^2)^{-1}\|q-q_j\|_{L^2(D)}^2$. [F8] therefore gives $\|K_\varepsilon-T_{\varepsilon,j}\|\to0$. By [F7], $K_\varepsilon$ is compact.

As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, step 1.2 gives $\|K-K_\varepsilon\|\le2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2\to0$. Applying [F7] again shows $K$ is compact. Step 1.1 independently gives the displayed norm estimate and compactness with the finite-measure Hilbert–Schmidt normalization.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. For every measure space and $1\le p\le\infty$, $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is complete. Every sequence converging in this norm has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to a measurable representative of its norm limit. For finite $p$ no pointwise convergence of the whole sequence is asserted.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Assume AC and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. Then $K_k:L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ is compact and
$$\|K_k\|\le\|G_k(x-y)q(y)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$

The proof supplies both the finite-measure Hilbert–Schmidt rescaling route required by the kernel interface and the singular-truncation/Schur route specified for this volume kernel. No uniqueness or outgoing-scattering solvability is asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a Banach space
over a fixed field $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $K:X\to X$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and put $A:=I-K$. Then:

1. $A$ is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case $A$ is
   boundedly invertible;
2. for every $y\in X$ the equation $Ax=y$ has a solution if and only if
   $\varphi(y)=0$ for every $\varphi\in\ker A^*$, the transpose
   $A^*=I-K^*$ acting on $X^*$
   ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]);
3. $\ker A$ and the cokernel $X/\operatorname{ran}A$
   ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]]) are finite dimensional with
   equal dimensions over $F$ ([[def-dimension]]).

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

On every measure space the pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ on complex $L^2$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$. Moreover,
$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

For each finite $m\ge0$, the same conclusions hold on tuples $F=(f_j)_{j<m}$, with pairing $B(F,G)=\sum_{j<m}\langle f_j,g_j\rangle$ and $\|F\|^2=\sum_{j<m}\|f_j\|_2^2$. For $G\ne0$, equality means $f_j=cg_j$ a.e. for every $j$, with one common scalar $c$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Thus, for $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume-potential integral is absolutely convergent: $\overline D$ is closed, so its complement contains a ball about $x$ disjoint from $D$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

This is a stipulated integral-equation model with the sign convention $(-\Delta-k^2)(u-f)=q u$ when the corresponding distributional Helmholtz equation is used. In the acoustic notation of Scherzer–Mindrinos, their equation $u=u_i-k^2\Phi*((1-n)u)$ corresponds to $q=k^2(n-1)$. No existence or uniqueness for all contrasts is asserted by this definition.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the defining integral of $\mathcal F_kv$ is absolutely convergent and $|\mathcal F_kv(\theta)|\le(4\pi)^{-1}\|qv\|_1$. Taking the supremum proves the norm bound; linearity follows from linearity of the integral.

For $\theta,\theta'\in S^2$, [F2] gives $|e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}-e^{-ik\theta'\cdot y}|\le |k|\,|y|\,|\theta-\theta'|$. Integrating against $|qv|/(4\pi)$ and using [F1] proves the stated Lipschitz bound and hence continuity in direction.

Fix $r\ge2R_0$, $\theta\in S^2$, and $y\in D$, and set $s:=|r\theta-y|$. Then $s\ge r-R_0\ge r/2$, $|r-s|\le R_0$, and
$$|s-(r-\theta\cdot y)|=\frac{|y|^2-(\theta\cdot y)^2}{s+r-\theta\cdot y}\le\frac{R_0^2}{r},$$
because the denominator is at least $(r-R_0)+(r-R_0)\ge r$. Therefore $|r/s-1|\le2R_0/r$ and, by [F2], $|e^{ik(s-r)}-e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}|\le |k|R_0^2/r$.

The integrand identity $r e^{-ikr}G_k(r\theta-y)=(4\pi)^{-1}(r/s)e^{ik(s-r)}$ and step 1.3 give a uniform pointwise error at most $(2R_0+|k|R_0^2)/(4\pi r)$. Integrating against $|qv|$, applying [F1], and taking the supremum over $\theta$ proves the far-field estimate.

$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

$(X,\overline{\mathcal{A}_0},\overline{\mu})$ be its completion. If
$f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is measurable with respect to
$\overline{\mathcal{A}_0}$, then there is an $\mathcal{A}_0$-measurable function
$g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f=g$ almost everywhere.

This representative is in Borel $L^2$ because the original extension is square integrable and the affine change multiplies its squared integral by the fixed positive factor $\operatorname{side}(Q)^{-3}$. Applying [F1] to its real and imaginary parts gives dyadic box step functions converging in Borel $L^2([0,1)^3)$, hence also in completed $L^2$. Pulling them back to $Q$ and restricting to $D$ preserves convergence up to the fixed affine measure factor. Every finite family of base-2 boxes is constant on the cells of a sufficiently fine common dyadic partition, so the restrictions belong to some $V_N$. Thus $\bigcup_NV_N$ is dense in $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$; the partitions are nested, so $V_N\subseteq V_{N+1}$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By step 1.2 choose $w\in V_m$ with $\|v-w\|_2<\varepsilon/2$. For every $N\ge m$, nesting gives $P_Nw=w$. Therefore $\|P_Nv-v\|_2\le\|P_N(v-w)\|_2+\|v-w\|_2\le2\|v-w\|_2<\varepsilon$, by step 1.1. Thus $P_Nv\to v$ in $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable, and choose a half-open cube $Q$ of positive side length containing $D$. Subdivide $Q$ into its nested dyadic cubes at mesh $h_N=2^{-N}\operatorname{side}(Q)$. Let $E_{N,j}=D\cap Q_{N,j}$ range over the finitely many cells of positive measure, let $V_N\subset L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ be the functions constant on each such cell, and define $P_N$ by replacing a function on each $E_{N,j}$ by its cell average. Then $P_N$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V_N$, $\|P_N\|\le1$, the spaces $V_N$ are increasing, and $P_Nv\to v$ in $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ for every $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$.

Assume AC and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. Then $K_k:L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ is compact and
$$\|K_k\|\le\|G_k(x-y)q(y)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$

The proof supplies both the finite-measure Hilbert–Schmidt rescaling route required by the kernel interface and the singular-truncation/Schur route specified for this volume kernel. No uniqueness or outgoing-scattering solvability is asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X\ne\{0\}$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), let $K:X\to X$
be compact, and let $(K_n)_{n\ge1}$ be bounded linear operators such that
$$\overline{\bigcup_{n\ge1}K_n(B_X)}$$
is compact for the closed unit ball $B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le1\}$ and
$K_nx\to Kx$ in norm for every $x\in X$. Suppose $I-K$ is injective. Then
there are $n_0\ge1$ and $C<\infty$ such that $I-K_n$ is boundedly invertible
for every $n\ge n_0$ and
$$\sup_{n\ge n_0}\|(I-K_n)^{-1}\|\le C.$$
For any $f,f_n\in X$, if $u$ and $u_n$ solve $(I-K)u=f$ and
$(I-K_n)u_n=f_n$, then for $n\ge n_0$,
$$\|u_n-u\|\le C\bigl(\|(K_n-K)u\|+\|f_n-f\|\bigr).$$
The theorem does not assert that $\|K_n-K\|\to0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D,q,k$ be as in [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]], let $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, and assume $0<|D|<\infty$. Let $P_N$ be the dyadic cell-average projection of [[lem-dyadic-cell-average-projections-converge-in-l2]], and put $K_N:=P_NK_k$ and $f_N:=P_Nf$. This is a finite-rank volume product-integration rule on $L^2(D)$; the projection and kernel convention are fixed by those definitions.

For each positive-measure cell $E_{N,j}$ set $\phi_{N,j}:=|E_{N,j}|^{-1/2}\mathbf1_{E_{N,j}}$. The exact product-cell weights and right-hand side are
$$A^{(N)}_{ij}:=\langle K_k\phi_{N,j},\phi_{N,i}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|E_{N,i}||E_{N,j}|}}\int_{E_{N,i}}\int_{E_{N,j}}G_k(x-y)q(y)\,dy\,dx,\qquad b^{(N)}_i:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|E_{N,i}|}}\int_{E_{N,i}}f(x)\,dx.$$
For each cell pair, the double integral is absolutely convergent: the kernel $G_k(x-y)q(y)$ is in $L^2(D\times D)$ and $\phi_{N,i}(x)\phi_{N,j}(y)$ has product $L^2$ norm one, so Cauchy--Schwarz makes their product integrable. Completed-product Fubini under Countable Choice then gives the displayed equality with the inner product.
The finite system is $(I-A^{(N)})c=b^{(N)}$, and its reconstruction is $u_N=\sum_jc_j\phi_{N,j}$. Equivalently, it solves $(I-K_N)u_N=f_N$ in $V_N$. Its far-field output is the exact cell integral
$$\mathcal F_N(c)(\theta):=\mathcal F_k[u_N](\theta)=\sum_j\frac{c_j}{4\pi\sqrt{|E_{N,j}|}}\int_{E_{N,j}}e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)\,dy.$$
A singular finite matrix has status `singular`; the definition makes no unconditional invertibility claim. The double integrals are taken over whole cell pairs, including diagonal pairs; no point value of $G_k$ at its singular diagonal is sampled. Finiteness is established by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]] and [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

The rule uses exact cell weights as a mathematical discretization. This definition makes no claim about floating-point evaluation or approximate cell weights.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D,q,k$ be as in [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]], with $0<|D|<\infty$, and put $R_0>\sup_{y\in D}|y|$. Then $\mathcal F_k:L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to C(S^2;\mathbb C)$ is linear and
$$\|\mathcal F_kv\|_\infty\le\frac{\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{|D|}}{4\pi}\|v\|_2.$$
It is Lipschitz in direction with constant at most $|k|R_0\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{|D|}\|v\|_2/(4\pi)$. For every $r\ge2R_0$, the exterior volume potential of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] satisfies
$$\sup_{\theta\in S^2}\left|r e^{-ikr}V_kv(r\theta)-\mathcal F_kv(\theta)\right|\le\frac{2R_0+|k|R_0^2}{4\pi r}\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{|D|}\|v\|_2.$$
Thus $\mathcal F_kv$ is the uniform far-field amplitude under the outgoing $e^{ikr}/r$ convention.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Assume countable choice. For every measure space and $1\le p\le\infty$, $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is complete. Every sequence converging in this norm has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to a measurable representative of its norm limit. For finite $p$ no pointwise convergence of the whole sequence is asserted.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom
of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]).** Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]). Then the following five conditions are equivalent.

- **(a)** $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
- **(b)** $(X,d)$ is countably compact ([[def-metric-compactness-variants]]).
- **(c)** $(X,d)$ is limit point compact.
- **(d)** $(X,d)$ is sequentially compact.
- **(e)** $(X,d)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and totally bounded
  ([[def-totally-bounded]]).

**The two hypotheses are not needed everywhere, and the statement should not be
read as if they were.** Of the implications assembled below, all but two are
theorems of ZF. Dependent choice is used only for "sequentially compact implies
totally bounded" ([[thm-sequentially-compact-implies-totally-bounded]]), and
countable choice only for "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]). Each is an upper bound on
the cost of the proof given in this library and not a claim of necessity; the
implication-by-implication account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

derivations.claim: Let $X=L^2(D;\mathbb C)$. Since $|D|>0$, $X\ne\{0\}$ (a normalized indicator of any positive-measure cell or subset is nonzero). By [F6] and AC, $X$ is a Banach space. [F2] gives compactness of $K_k$, and the assumed injectivity makes the Fredholm premise of [F3] applicable once the approximation hypotheses are checked.
By [F1] and [F4], $K_N=P_NK_k$ is bounded linear and $\|K_N\|\le\|K_k\|$. For every $v\in X$, [F1] applied to $K_kv$ gives $K_Nv=P_NK_kv\to K_kv$ in norm.

Let $B_X$ be the closed unit ball and $C=\overline{K_k(B_X)}$. Compactness in [F2] makes $C$ compact. Strong convergence $P_Nz\to z$ from [F1] is uniform for $z\in C$: given $\epsilon>0$, cover $C$ by finitely many $\epsilon/3$ balls with centers $z_1,\ldots,z_s$, choose $N_0$ so that $\|P_Nz_j-z_j\|<\epsilon/3$ for every center and $N\ge N_0$, then use $\|P_N\|\le1$ to get $\sup_{z\in C}\|P_Nz-z\|<\epsilon$. To show the tail union is totally bounded, start with any radius $\delta>0$, apply this uniform estimate with $\epsilon=\delta/3$, and cover $C$ by finitely many $\delta/3$ balls; each $P_Nz$ with $N\ge N_0$ then lies within $2\delta/3$ of one of their centers. Thus $\bigcup_{N\ge N_0}P_N(C)$ is totally bounded. Each of the finitely many earlier sets $P_N(C)$ is compact as a continuous image of $C$, hence totally bounded. Their union $U:=\bigcup_{N\ge1}P_N(C)$ is totally bounded. Its closure is totally bounded too: for any $\delta>0$, take a finite $\delta/2$-net of $U$; every point of $\overline U$ is within $\delta/2$ of some point of $U$, which is within $\delta/2$ of a net center. The closure is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $\overline U$ converges in the Banach space $X$ from step 1.1, and closedness of $\overline U$ keeps that limit in $\overline U$. By [F6], $\overline U$ is compact. Since $K_N(B_X)=P_NK_k(B_X)\subset P_N(C)$, the family $(K_N)$ is collectively compact in the precise sense required by [F3].

Now all hypotheses of [F3] hold by steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1. Therefore there are $N_0$ and a uniform $C$ such that $I-K_N$ is invertible for $N\ge N_0$ and its solutions satisfy $\|u_N-u\|_2\le C\bigl(\|(K_N-K_k)u\|_2+\|f_N-f\|_2\bigr)=C\bigl(\|(P_N-I)K_ku\|_2+\|(P_N-I)f\|_2\bigr)$. The right side tends to zero by [F1].

For $N\ge N_0$, the full-space solution satisfies $u_N=f_N+P_NK_ku_N\in V_N$. In the normalized cell-indicator basis of [F4], its equation is exactly $(I-A^{(N)})c=b^{(N)}$. If that finite matrix had a nonzero null vector, its corresponding nonzero element of $V_N$ would be in the kernel of $I-K_N$, contradicting invertibility; thus the matrix is nonsingular and its reconstruction is the unique operator solution. Finally [F5] gives the stated far-field bound, and step 3.1 makes its right side tend to zero.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Use the unit sphere $S^2$ and its polar surface measure $d\sigma$ from [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. For each integer $\ell\ge0$, let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the complex vector space of restrictions to $S^2$ of homogeneous degree-$\ell$ polynomials $P$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the Euclidean harmonic equation $\Delta P=0$. For complex-valued polynomials or functions, $\Delta$ and its polar-coordinate formulas act componentwise on real and imaginary parts. In polar coordinates $x=r\omega$, define $\Delta_{S^2}$ by
$$\Delta_{\mathbb R^3}=\partial_r^2+\frac2r\partial_r+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{S^2},$$
equivalently $\Delta_{S^2}=\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\partial_\theta)+\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\phi^2$ away from the poles. Thus if $Y\in\mathcal H_\ell$ is the restriction of $P$, then $\Delta_{S^2}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y$.

For $\ell\ge0$, define the normalized zonal polynomial $P_\ell(t)$ to be the degree-$\ell$ polynomial satisfying
$$ (1-t^2)P_\ell''(t)-2tP_\ell'(t)+\ell(\ell+1)P_\ell(t)=0,\qquad P_\ell(1)=1.$$
The later harmonic-basis lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this normalized polynomial and identifies it with the usual Legendre convention.

The term **partial wave of degree $\ell$** means the $\mathcal H_\ell$ component of an angular expansion in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma;\mathbb C)$. Completeness, orthogonality, finite dimension, and the evaluation bound for these components are established in [[lem-spherical-harmonics-form-complete-basis-and-addition-formula]].

For a radial field $u(r,\omega)$, its degree-$\ell$ component is written $u_\ell(r,\omega)\in\mathcal H_\ell$; any orthonormal basis within this finite-dimensional space gives the equivalent scalar mode equations. The definition does not select such a basis globally.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For a bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, or the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ class, and real $u,v\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, $$\int_\Omega(v\Delta u-u\Delta v)\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}(v\partial_\nu u-u\partial_\nu v)\,dS.$$ The face convention and finiteness are those of the first Green identity; every normal is outward from Omega, including normals on holes.

If $A\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$ is a unital real function algebra and $\overline A$ is its uniform closure, then $u\in\overline A$ implies $|u|\in\overline A$; consequently $u\vee v$ and $u\wedge v$ lie in $\overline A$ whenever $u,v$ do.
Assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). If $\mu$ is a Radon measure on an LCH space $X$ and $1\le p<\infty$, then $C_c(X)$ is dense in $L^p(\mu)$.

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every Borel measure finite on compact sets on a second-countable LCH space is regular.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). A subset
$W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when

- **(W1)** $0_V \in W$;
- **(W2)** $W$ is closed under the vector addition: $u, v \in W$ implies
  $u + v \in W$;
- **(W3)** $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication: $\lambda \in F$ and
  $v \in W$ imply $\lambda v \in W$.

Every vector space $V$ has the two **trivial linear subspaces** $\{0_V\}$ and $V$
itself; a linear subspace $W$ with $W \ne V$ is called **proper**.

**The restricted operations are the required data, and $W$ is a vector space.**
By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation
$W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map
$F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector
space over $F$:

- axioms (V2)–(V5) are equations required of elements of $W$, which are in
  particular elements of $V$, so they are inherited from $V$; likewise
  associativity and commutativity of the restricted addition;
- $0_V$ lies in $W$ by (W1) and is a two-sided identity for the restricted
  addition, since it is one in $V$;
- for $v \in W$ the vector $(-1_F)v$ lies in $W$ by (W3), and
  $(-1_F)v = -v$ ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so $-v \in W$
  and $v + (-v) = 0_V$ holds in $W$.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

On every measure space the pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ on complex $L^2$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$. Moreover,
$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

For each finite $m\ge0$, the same conclusions hold on tuples $F=(f_j)_{j<m}$, with pairing $B(F,G)=\sum_{j<m}\langle f_j,g_j\rangle$ and $\|F\|^2=\sum_{j<m}\|f_j\|_2^2$. For $G\ne0$, equality means $f_j=cg_j$ a.e. for every $j$, with one common scalar $c$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.
If $A\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$ is unital and separates points, then for distinct $x,y\in K$ and reals $r,s$ there is $g\in A$ with $g(x)=r$ and $g(y)=s$.

For $r\ge0$, put $\overline B_3(0,r):=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, extending the positive-radius notation of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] to $r=0$. This closed three-dimensional ball has volume $4\pi r^3/3$.

derivations.claim: If $P_\ell(x)=r^\ell Y(\omega)$ is homogeneous and harmonic, the polar Laplacian convention in [F1] gives $0=\Delta P_\ell=r^{\ell-2}(\ell(\ell+1)Y+\Delta_{S^2}Y)$. Hence $-\Delta_{S^2}Y=\ell(\ell+1)Y$.

Let $\mathcal P_n$ be the homogeneous complex polynomials of degree $n$ in three variables, with monomial basis of size $\binom{n+2}{2}$. For homogeneous $R_m$ of degree $m$, direct differentiation gives $\Delta(|x|^{2a}R_m)=2a(2m+2a+1)|x|^{2a-2}R_m+|x|^{2a}\Delta R_m$. Given $S\in\mathcal P_{n-2}$, put $J=\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor$, $c_j=2(j+1)(2n-2j-1)$, $b_0=1/c_0$, and $b_j=-b_{j-1}/c_j$ for $1\le j\le J$. Then $Q=\sum_{j=0}^Jb_j|x|^{2(j+1)}\Delta^jS\in\mathcal P_n$ satisfies $\Delta Q=S$: the coefficient of $|x|^{2j}\Delta^jS$ is $b_jc_j+b_{j-1}=0$ for $j\ge1$, the $S$ coefficient is $b_0c_0=1$, and $\Delta^{J+1}S=0$. Thus $\Delta:\mathcal P_n\to\mathcal P_{n-2}$ is onto. By [F5], its harmonic kernel has dimension $\binom{n+2}{2}-\binom n2=2n+1$ for $n\ge2$; for $n=0,1$ all homogeneous polynomials are harmonic and have dimensions $1,3$. Restriction to $S^2$ is injective because homogeneity recovers $P(r\omega)=r^nP(\omega)$, so $\dim\mathcal H_n=2n+1$.

Let $P_\ell,Q_m$ be homogeneous harmonic polynomials of degrees $\ell,m$. Apply [F2] on the unit ball to the real and imaginary components of $P_\ell,\overline{Q_m}$. Their volume Laplacians vanish, while homogeneity gives outward normal derivatives $\partial_
u P_\ell=\ell P_\ell$ and $\partial_
u\overline{Q_m}=m\overline{Q_m}$ on $S^2$. Therefore $(\ell-m)\int_{S^2}P_\ell(\omega)\overline{Q_m(\omega)}d\sigma(\omega)=0$. If $\ell
e m$, this proves orthogonality.

For $P\in\mathcal P_n$, define $H=P+\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}a_j|x|^{2j}\Delta^jP$, where $a_0=1$ and $a_{j+1}=-a_j/[2(j+1)(2n-2j-1)]$. The differentiation identity in step 1.2 shows that the coefficients of each $|x|^{2j}\Delta^{j+1}P$ cancel in $\Delta H$, so $H$ is harmonic. Since $P-H$ is divisible by $|x|^2$, restriction to $S^2$ writes $P|_{S^2}$ as an element of $\mathcal H_n$ plus the restriction of a homogeneous degree-$(n-2)$ polynomial. Induction on degree decomposes every polynomial restriction into a finite sum of spherical harmonics.

Fix $\ell$. By [F10], the $L^2$ inner product is positive definite on the finite-dimensional space of continuous restrictions, so finite-dimensional Gram--Schmidt gives an orthonormal basis. The sum $Z_\ell$ is independent of this basis because a unitary change of basis preserves the sum of rank-one coordinate kernels. For $R\in SO(3)$ and Borel $E\subseteq S^2$, the polar-surface definition represents $\sigma(E)$ as three times the Lebesgue measure of its unit radial cone $C_E=\{r\omega:0<r\le1,\ \omega\in E\}$. Since $R$ is a homeomorphism, $RE$ is Borel, $RC_E=C_{RE}$, and $|\det R|=1$; [F7] therefore gives $\sigma(RE)=\sigma(E)$. If $P$ is homogeneous and harmonic of degree $\ell$, then $P\circ R^{-1}$ is homogeneous of the same degree and remains harmonic: termwise differentiation of monomials in the real and imaginary parts gives $\partial_i\partial_i(P\circ R^{-1})(x)=\sum_{a,b}(R^{-1})_{ai}(R^{-1})_{bi}(\partial_a\partial_bP)(R^{-1}x)$; summing over $i$ and using $R^{-1}(R^{-1})^T=I$ proves $\Delta(P\circ R^{-1})=(\Delta P)\circ R^{-1}=0$. Thus composition with $R^{-1}$ is unitary on $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ and preserves $\mathcal H_\ell$; the rotated basis is again orthonormal, so basis independence gives $Z_\ell(R\omega,R\eta)=Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)$. In particular $Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)$ is constant because rotations act transitively on $S^2$. Integrating the diagonal gives $\int_{S^2}Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)d\sigma=2\ell+1$. Polar coordinates applied to the unit ball and its volume $4\pi/3$ ([[cor-volume-of-a-closed-three-ball]]) give $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, so the diagonal constant is $(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. Cauchy–Schwarz for the finite coefficient vector yields the displayed evaluation bound.

Let $A$ be the restrictions of real polynomials to $S^2$; constants, sums, and products show that it is a unital real algebra, and coordinate functions separate distinct points. Fix $f\in C(S^2;\mathbb R)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For each fixed $\eta\in S^2$, form the family of open sets $U_p:=\{\omega:p(\omega)>f(\omega)-\varepsilon/2\}$ for all $p\in A$ with $p(\eta)=f(\eta)$. This family covers $S^2$: for each $\omega$, [F8] supplies an interpolant $p$ with $p(\eta)=f(\eta)$ and $p(\omega)=f(\omega)$, using the constant polynomial when $\omega=\eta$. By [F9], compactness gives a finite subcover corresponding to $p_1,\ldots,p_s$. Their maximum $g_\eta\in\overline A$ by [F3] satisfies $g_\eta(\eta)=f(\eta)$ and $g_\eta>f-\varepsilon/2$ everywhere. This proves the existence of such a function for every $\eta$ without choosing a family indexed by $S^2$. Define the set $\mathcal G:=\{g\in\overline A:g>f-\varepsilon/2\text{ on }S^2\}$ and the open sets $V_g:=\{\omega:g(\omega)<f(\omega)+\varepsilon/2\}$ for $g\in\mathcal G$. The functions whose existence was just proved show that these sets cover $S^2$, so [F9] gives a finite subcover $V_{g_1},\ldots,V_{g_t}$. The minimum $h:=\min_i g_i$ lies in $\overline A$ by [F3] and satisfies $f-\varepsilon/2<h<f+\varepsilon/2$ everywhere. Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, $f\in\overline A$ and the real polynomial restrictions are dense in $C(S^2;\mathbb R)$. Applying this to real and imaginary parts gives density of complex polynomial restrictions in $C(S^2;\mathbb C)$. By [F4] and [F9], $d\sigma$ is Radon and $C(S^2;\mathbb C)=C_c(S^2;\mathbb C)$ is dense in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma;\mathbb C)$. Step 2.2 therefore implies that the span of the mutually orthogonal spaces $\mathcal H_\ell$ is dense in $L^2$.

For fixed $\eta$, rotations fixing $\eta$ leave $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)$ invariant. Writing an invariant polynomial in coordinates parallel and perpendicular to $\eta$ shows it is a polynomial in $t=\omega\cdot\eta$ on $S^2$. Since it belongs to $\mathcal H_\ell$, the spherical-Laplacian formula in the Definition gives $(1-t^2)p''-2tp'+\ell(\ell+1)p=0$ for this polynomial $p$. If $p(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}c_jt^j$, coefficient comparison gives $(j+2)(j+1)c_{j+2}+[\ell(\ell+1)-j(j+1)]c_j=0$ for $0\le j<\ell$; downward recursion determines every coefficient from $c_\ell$, and a nonzero solution cannot have degree $d<\ell$ because its leading coefficient would be multiplied by $\ell(\ell+1)-d(d+1)\ne0$. Thus polynomial solutions of degree at most $\ell$ form a one-dimensional space of degree exactly $\ell$. By step 2.3, $p(1)=Z_\ell(\eta,\eta)=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)>0$. Consequently $P_\ell(t):=4\pi p(t)/(2\ell+1)$ is the unique degree-$\ell$ solution with $P_\ell(1)=1$ from the Definition, and $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\eta)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Thus, for $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume-potential integral is absolutely convergent: $\overline D$ is closed, so its complement contains a ball about $x$ disjoint from $D$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

For an integer $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, and an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, put $\mathcal D_K=\{\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K\}$, using [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. For integers $m\ge0$ set

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Also [F7] gives $|\Phi_k(x)|=1/(4\pi|x|)$, whose integral over each centered ball is finite by [F2]. Hence $\Phi_k\in L^1_{\rm loc}$ and [F6] supplies its regular distribution. Point evaluation is continuous by [F5], so $\delta_0$ is also a distribution. Thus $(-\Delta-k^2)\Phi_k=0$ away from the origin as a classical equation and the distributional pairing in the next step is defined.

Choose an outer sphere beyond $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ and apply [F3] on the annulus between it and radius $\epsilon$. Apply the real identity to the four real/imaginary pairings to obtain the complex bilinear identity. The outer boundary term is zero, and the inner boundary orientation yields $\int_{|x|>\epsilon}\Phi_k(x)(-\Delta-k^2)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{|x|=\epsilon}(\Phi_k\partial_r\varphi-\varphi\partial_r\Phi_k)\,dS$. The first term is $O(\epsilon)$ since $\Phi_k=O(\epsilon^{-1})$ and the sphere area is $4\pi\epsilon^2$. From the derivative formula in step 1.1 and the exponential series, $e^{ik\epsilon}(ik\epsilon-1)=-1+O(\epsilon^2)$, so $\partial_r\Phi_k=-1/(4\pi\epsilon^2)+O(1)$. Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Thus, for $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume-potential integral is absolutely convergent: $\overline D$ is closed, so its complement contains a ball about $x$ disjoint from $D$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

This is a stipulated integral-equation model with the sign convention $(-\Delta-k^2)(u-f)=q u$ when the corresponding distributional Helmholtz equation is used. In the acoustic notation of Scherzer–Mindrinos, their equation $u=u_i-k^2\Phi*((1-n)u)$ corresponds to $q=k^2(n-1)$. No existence or uniqueness for all contrasts is asserted by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. For real $k$, let $\Phi_k(x)=e^{ik|x|}/(4\pi|x|)$ for $x\ne0$. In the sense of distributions on $\mathbb R^3$,
$$(-\Delta-k^2)\Phi_k=\delta_0.$$
Here $\delta_0$ is the point-mass distribution defined by $\langle\delta_0,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(0)$ for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$. Consequently, if $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ has bounded support, the integral $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi_k(x-y)g(y)\,dy$ is absolutely finite for almost every $x$. Define $V$ by this integral almost everywhere (and arbitrarily on the exceptional null set). Then $V\in L^1_{\rm loc}$ and $(-\Delta-k^2)V=g$ distributionally.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Use the unit sphere $S^2$ and its polar surface measure $d\sigma$ from [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. For each integer $\ell\ge0$, let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the complex vector space of restrictions to $S^2$ of homogeneous degree-$\ell$ polynomials $P$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the Euclidean harmonic equation $\Delta P=0$. For complex-valued polynomials or functions, $\Delta$ and its polar-coordinate formulas act componentwise on real and imaginary parts. In polar coordinates $x=r\omega$, define $\Delta_{S^2}$ by
$$\Delta_{\mathbb R^3}=\partial_r^2+\frac2r\partial_r+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{S^2},$$
equivalently $\Delta_{S^2}=\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\partial_\theta)+\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\phi^2$ away from the poles. Thus if $Y\in\mathcal H_\ell$ is the restriction of $P$, then $\Delta_{S^2}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y$.

For $\ell\ge0$, define the normalized zonal polynomial $P_\ell(t)$ to be the degree-$\ell$ polynomial satisfying
$$ (1-t^2)P_\ell''(t)-2tP_\ell'(t)+\ell(\ell+1)P_\ell(t)=0,\qquad P_\ell(1)=1.$$
The later harmonic-basis lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this normalized polynomial and identifies it with the usual Legendre convention.

The term **partial wave of degree $\ell$** means the $\mathcal H_\ell$ component of an angular expansion in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma;\mathbb C)$. Completeness, orthogonality, finite dimension, and the evaluation bound for these components are established in [[lem-spherical-harmonics-form-complete-basis-and-addition-formula]].

For a radial field $u(r,\omega)$, its degree-$\ell$ component is written $u_\ell(r,\omega)\in\mathcal H_\ell$; any orthonormal basis within this finite-dimensional space gives the equivalent scalar mode equations. The definition does not select such a basis globally.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Use $\mathcal H_\ell$ from [[def-spherical-harmonic-partial-wave-conventions]]. For every $\ell\ge0$, $\dim_\mathbb C\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$; the spaces $\mathcal H_\ell$ are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma;\mathbb C)$ and their algebraic sum is dense there. Thus they give a complete orthogonal spherical-harmonic expansion. For any orthonormal basis $Y_{\ell 1},\ldots,Y_{\ell,2\ell+1}$ of $\mathcal H_\ell$, the basis-independent reproducing kernel
$$Z_\ell(\omega,\eta):=\sum_{m=1}^{2\ell+1}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\eta)}$$
satisfies $Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. In particular,
$$|g(\omega)|\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_{L^2(S^2)}\qquad(g\in\mathcal H_\ell).$$
For fixed $\eta$, rotational invariance makes $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)$ a degree-$\ell$ zonal polynomial of $\omega\cdot\eta$; normalizing $P_\ell(1)=1$ gives the usual addition identity $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\eta)$.

For the functions of [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]], define
$$L_\ell y:=y''+\frac2z y'+\left(1-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{z^2}\right)y\qquad(z>0).$$
Then $L_\ell j_\ell=L_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}=0$, and for $y=j,h^{(1)}$,
$$y_{\ell+1}(z)=\frac{\ell}{z}y_\ell(z)-y_\ell'(z),\qquad y_\ell'(z)=y_{\ell-1}(z)-\frac{\ell+1}{z}y_\ell(z)\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
The regular-origin and outgoing-infinity normalizations are
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{z^\ell}{(2\ell+1)!!}+O(z^{\ell+2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=-i(2\ell-1)!!z^{-\ell-1}(1+O(z))\quad(z\downarrow0),$$
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{\sin(z-\ell\pi/2)}z+O(z^{-2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}\frac{e^{iz}}z+O(z^{-2})\quad(z\to\infty),$$
where $(-1)!!:=1$. Their Wronskian is
$$j_\ell(z)(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)-j_\ell'(z)h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=\frac{i}{z^2}.$$

The boundedness of $Q$ and continuity of $u$ on the compact ball imply $qu\in L^1(B_R)$ with bounded support, so [F1] applies. Since $u^{\rm inc}$ solves $(-\Delta-k^2)u^{\rm inc}=0$, [F1] gives $\Delta u+(k^2+Q(r))u=0$ in $0<r<R$. For fixed $r$, multiply the polar Laplacian identity by $\overline{Y_{\ell m}}$, integrate over $S^2$, and integrate the angular Laplacian by parts; the periodic azimuthal boundary terms cancel and the polar boundary terms vanish with the factor $\sin\theta$. By [F2], the angular term is $-\ell(\ell+1)$ times the mode coefficient $a_{\ell m}(r):=w_{\ell m}(r)/r$. Hence
$$a_{\ell m}''+\frac2r a_{\ell m}'+\left(k^2+Q(r)-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}\right)a_{\ell m}=0.$$
Substitution of $w=ra$ yields the asserted reduced ODE.

The stated origin condition is precisely the regular branch condition for this reduced mode and is retained as a hypothesis, so no singular solution is admitted. Because $u$ and its first derivatives are continuous across $r=R$, integration against the fixed smooth harmonic gives continuity of $w_{\ell m}$ and $w_{\ell m}'$ there.

Outside $B_R$, the scattered field $V$ solves the free Helmholtz equation by [F1]. Its angular coefficient $v_{\ell m}(r)=\int_{S^2}V(r\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega)}d\sigma$ solves the free radial equation, whose independent solutions are $j_\ell(kr)$ and $h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ by the nonzero Wronskian in [F4]; write $v_{\ell m}=a j_\ell(kr)+b h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$. The uniform radiation condition, integrated against the bounded $Y_{\ell m}$, gives $r(v'_{\ell m}-ikv_{\ell m})\to0$. Put $\vartheta=kr-\ell\pi/2$ and $c=(-i)^{\ell+1}$. The derivative recurrence in [F4] for $\ell\ge1$, and direct differentiation of the base functions for $\ell=0$, give $j_\ell'(z)=\cos(z-\ell\pi/2)/z+O(z^{-2})$ and $(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)=ic e^{iz}/z+O(z^{-2})$, so $r(\partial_r-ik)j_\ell(kr)=e^{-i\vartheta}+O(r^{-1})$ while $r(\partial_r-ik)h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)=O(r^{-1})$. Thus the radiation limit forces $a=0$, and the scattered mode is $\beta_{\ell m}h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$. Adding the stipulated incident mode gives the exterior expression in the Statement.

The interior/exterior continuity of the total mode and its radial derivative from step 1.2 gives the two matching equalities at $R$. Completeness in [F3] makes these modal statements the corresponding partial-wave decomposition, without asserting that the mode equations alone solve the full inverse or uniqueness problem.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $(\Pi_Lg_k)(d)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\frac{2\ell+1}{2}\int_{-1}^1e^{ikt}P_\ell(t)dt$. For a fixed polynomial $P_\ell$, integration by parts gives $\left|\int_{-1}^{1}e^{ikt}P_\ell(t)dt\right|\le\frac{|P_\ell(1)|+|P_\ell(-1)|+\int_{-1}^1|P_\ell'(t)|dt}{k}$. Summing finitely many terms yields $|(\Pi_Lg_k)(d)|\le C_L/k$ for a finite constant $C_L$ independent of $k$.

Since $|g_k(d)|=|e^{ik}|=1$, step 1.1 and the reverse triangle inequality give $|g_k(d)-(\Pi_Lg_k)(d)|\ge1-C_L/k\to1$. If integer cutoffs $L(k)$ failed to tend to infinity as $k\to\infty$, there would be $L_0$ and a sequence $k_n\to\infty$ with $L(k_n)\le L_0$; the finite maximum $C=\max_{0\le j\le L_0}C_j$ would give the same lower bound $1-C/k_n\to1$ along that sequence. Thus a cutoff with uniform error bounded by any fixed $\varepsilon<1$ for all sufficiently large $k$ must satisfy $L(k)\to\infty$.
